content:
KETTLE Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia after a trio of affairs that include an alleged Chinese spy and two of his subordinates, turning the week into one that's shaken the tech sector.

You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live.

What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? Will other chipmakers take advantage of the chaos to surpass the Geforce maker? Will Jensen be the one to put a pin to the AI bubble?

Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, systems editor Tobias Mann, and reporter Dan Robinson to talk about the Jensen Huang affair(s) and how the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names could reshape the entire industry on this week's episode.

A lightly edited transcript is included below:

Brandon (00:01)

Hey everyone and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and the big news on the tech industry's mind this week is the ouster of Nvidia founder, CEO, president, and board member Jensen Huang over allegations that he not only had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but also at least two Nvidia employees who were his subordinates.

Nvidia's been shaped into one of the most valuable companies in the world over the past thirty-three years, and Huang has played a pivotal, if not the pivotal, role in that ascension, meaning his controversial departure is going to rock the industry, if not the greater world. With me to discuss this is our systems editor Tobias Mann and Reg reporter Dan Robinson. Thanks to you both for coming on.

Dan Robinson (00:42)

Hi.

Tobias Mann (00:43)

Good to be here.

Brandon (00:43)

Quite the week, huh? It seems like we went from Jensen’s just going to survive this spy kerfuffle to the board basically seeming to demand his resignation in the course of a few days, right? So Dan, bring us up to speed on the timeline here, what happened?

Dan Robinson (01:01)

Well, it all happened over the last couple of weeks. That was when the story first surfaced, or it was first reported in the media, of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who happened to work for this company in Singapore that bought a lot of Nvidia's products.

Brandon (01:30)

Right, company was Megaspeed, right? And her name's Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, coincidence.

Dan Robinson (01:36)

So it's all happened fairly quickly, but like you say, at the start of this week, it all seemed like Jensen could weather the storm. We were discussing this in our editorial chat and we thought that basically there isn't really anybody who could replace him, or so we thought. He practically is Nvidia, and it's been his vision that's driven the company for so long. But then he came out and he confessed and said he was sorry to all the Nvidia employees. Then the second affair came to light and very quickly, on November 11th actually, Wednesday, he handed in his resignation and it was accepted by the board. So we got to hear about it yesterday [Thursday] when they announced it and it was filed with the SEC.

Brandon (03:03)

And since then a third affair has come out, right? The New York Times published a finding.

Tobias Mann (03:06)

Just a few hours later, yeah.

Dan Robinson (03:08)

It seems so. Makes you wonder how many others may be about to come out in the following days.

Brandon (03:13)

We're not going to speculate, but my gosh, it seems like that leather jacket really made him irresistible. It’s kind of crazy, right? It seems like the internal affairs with Nvidia employees are the ones that sort of broke the board's back, right? The spy affair seemed like it was kind of like…. Apparently American authorities have basically said they've found no direct evidence to say she is a spy.

Dan Robinson (03:44)

Exactly.

Brandon (03:45)

It could just be that she runs a chip company too, or at least a company that is dealing in servers and datacenters. So she has a business reason beyond politics to potentially want to get involved with Jensen. What do you guys think? Was it the internal elements that finally kind of broke the camel's back here and forced the board to act?

Dan Robinson (04:08)

I think that was the final straw. I think quite possibly he could have weathered the storm as we were saying, if it had just been the one affair outside the business.

Brandon (04:20)

Outside the business, right? Because now like you were saying, Tobias, not only do you have potentially an international spy affair, but you also have an HR issue to contend with.

Tobias Mann (04:29)

Right. And I do think that the board could wave their hands around an alleged honeypot scenario. “He was targeted, this was a deliberate act, they preyed on his insecurity.”

Brandon (04:44)

“It wasn't as big as it's made out to be in the media.”

Tobias Mann (04:47)

They could make up any number of excuses that they wanted in order to wave their hands over it and keep him CEO or if their arms were twisted by US intelligence services they could have taken him out of an executive role and pushed him into a chairmanship. They had options.

And then you had the HR kerfuffle of him allegedly sleeping with another employee. And at that point now there's a pattern. I do sort of question once the news came out that he had an extramarital affair with an employee, whether or not that had influenced him being targeted by Megaspeed and or the Chinese intelligence service, assuming those allegations prove out.

Brandon (05:42)

We don't know the timeline on one or the other, do we?

Tobias Mann (05:46)

Right, no. And so it could be that the Chinese intelligence service became aware that this was an avenue that could be exploited and they took it. It's not lost on anybody that he spent most of the last year and a half lobbying to get his chips back into China. And largely successfully on the US side of things. It's been held up by Beijing, which kind of undermines that theory a little bit.

Brandon (06:22)

It seems like if she was a spy doing China's bidding and he managed to get the Trump administration to allow those older chips in, then Beijing wouldn't have been like, “No, screw you, we're making our own….”

Tobias Mann (06:34)

But there's the other allegation here, which was that Alice Huang and Megaspeed were smuggling GPUs. Their operation in Singapore was set up such to bring more modern GPUs into the market. And so it could have been that Beijing all of this is alleged didn't really care for its model labs getting old hardware. So they could appear to be blocking us and promoting their own chips while smuggling in more advanced silicon from Nvidia through Singapore.

Brandon (07:10)

Through Alice Huang's company, essentially, right? So I know Jensen's going to be appearing before Congress to talk about all this, right? This is not over by a long shot, right?

Tobias Mann (07:26)

So, I don't think that we should play up the gray market and the black market side of the GPU smuggling operation too much. I highly doubt Jensen knew anything about that, other than he was aware that it happens. But gray market and black market smuggling, as anybody who's worked in the electronics and the technology field will know is nothing new.

When I was a young kid in college, gray market cameras, if you needed a new camera, was a great way to save a couple hundred bucks on a camera so long as you weren't expecting a warranty to come with it. So I wouldn't read too much into the smuggling side of things. I think that's happening, but I don't think Jensen's involved at all.

It's hard to ignore the fact that he spent the last year and a half lobbying Washington to allow chips into China, more powerful chips into China. And even prior to that, he had instructed his engineers to develop China-specific accelerators and cut down owned fuse off cores, whatever it took in order to limbo under export controls. And it was not particularly popular with the last administration. Gina Raimondo openly criticized Nvidia about how they were taking the spirit of the law out of context and Nvidia pushed back a little bit about that.

Dan Robinson (08:56)

That's right. She did say at one point that whatever Nvidia did to get around the rules, they were going to change them to block him.

Tobias Mann (09:08)

And she eventually walked that back a little bit, because the rules are there, and so you can't really get too upset with somebody for trying to abide by the rules. Was Nvidia following the spirit of it? No.

Brandon (09:18)

Sure. That's a huge potential market for Nvidia, right? China is a massive market and they have a huge appetite for chips, right?

Tobias Mann (09:29)

In one quarter They wrote off ten and a half billion dollars of potential profits because they could not ship H20s to China because the Trump administration kneejerked.

Brandon (09:38)

I remember when that story came out. That was a huge amount of money, right? How much of their market is Singapore in that area? It's some massive chunk of change.

Tobias Mann (09:50)

And Dan, you probably are aware of this as well. So there's a lot of companies that operate out of Singapore but don't actually have data centers there because it's not a particularly power-dense area for them. And so there's a lot of companies that, if you look at it at face value, looks like they're importing a lot of GPUs to Singapore, but the GPUs don't dor the most part don't actually make it there.

Brandon (10:21)

They're ending up in Malaysia.

Tobias Mann (10:22)

Except perhaps in the case of Megaspeed.

Brandon (10:24)

I think Simon [Sharwood] wrote a piece recently, I think it was actually just yesterday, where he mentioned that in one case, Singaporean buyers sometimes account for over twenty percent of the quarterly revenue for Nvidia. So that's a huge market, right? Whether or not those chips are ending up in Singapore or China or some other country that's operating as a territorial expansion of Singapore for serving data centers to them, that's a lot of money. And that market could grow immensely. So, there's a fair argument to be made there that in Jensen's just being a capitalist, right? He sees a market opportunity. He's going to try to take it, it's not a conspiracy. It's not necessarily that the company's acting in collusion with China to circumvent imports. It's just, well, we got this opportunity, so we're going to follow the letter of the law, not the spirit. I don't think it's necessarily fair to fault Nvidia for that.

Dan Robinson (11:20)

And Simon wrote [the] story which was about the Singaporean authorities saying that they were having a very hard time getting cooperation from the US authorities when they were investigating Megaspeed. So it does make you wonder if this really is a spying thing or if they're really worried about the smuggling, why were they not cooperating with the Singaporean authorities over this?

Brandon (11:54)

Right. Right.

Dan Robinson (11:55)

There's something else going on there, isn't there?

Brandon (11:58)

Very possibly. So OK, so more broadly, stepping back from just Nvidia and its trials and tribulations as one of the world's most largely successful companies, Tobias, you watch the chip industry. It's your thing here at the Reg. And watching chips obviously nowadays means watching Nvidia. I'm sure this is going to have an impact on the AI industry, the tech industry. And possibly beyond, right? So what have you been hearing from people you talk to, from other companies, from Nvidia itself, that is going to point to how this is going to impact the space?

Tobias Mann (12:41)

I just saw this morning, I think it was Wired had a piece out, that there's some disbelief and
